before.content_html:
Why Sound Creation Matters

Sound creation is the process of producing audio specifically designed for use in media. Without carefully created sound, a film would feel flat, a video game would lack immersion, and an advertisement would fail to grab attention. Understanding the different forms of media and types of sound creation is the starting point for this unit.

Forms of Media Using Sound Creation

Sound creation is used across a wide range of media. Each form has its own requirements, but all rely on carefully designed audio to enhance the audience’s experience.

Key Fact

The ten forms of media you must know are: radio broadcasts, movies, TV shows, video games, advertisements, jingles, podcasts, animations, theatre, and installations.

Radio broadcasts rely entirely on sound — music, speech, and effects must tell the whole story without any visual support. Movies and TV shows use sound to build atmosphere, convey emotion, and guide the viewer’s attention. Video games require interactive sound that responds to the player’s actions in real time.

Advertisements use short, punchy sound design to make products memorable. A jingle is a specific type of sound creation — a brief, catchy tune designed to stick in the listener’s mind and associate with a product or brand.

Podcasts use voice recording, music beds, and effects to create engaging audio-only content. Animations need all sounds to be created from scratch because there is no live-action audio to capture. Theatre uses live and pre-recorded sound effects and music to support performances. Installations are immersive art or exhibition spaces that use sound to create an environment or atmosphere for visitors.

Types of Sound Creation

There are six main types of sound creation. Each serves a different purpose within a media production.

Foley

Foley is the art of creating realistic, everyday sounds in a studio. Foley artists watch the visual footage and perform the sounds in sync — for example, walking on gravel to create footstep sounds, or crumpling paper to simulate fire. These sounds are recorded and layered into the final production to make it feel real.

Ambience

Ambience (also called atmosphere or room tone) is the background sound that sets the scene. It tells the audience where and when the action takes place. A busy city street has traffic and voices. A forest has birdsong and rustling leaves. Without ambience, a scene feels unnaturally silent and disconnected.

Dialogue

Dialogue is recorded speech between characters. In film and TV, dialogue is captured on set using boom microphones and lavalier mics, then cleaned and balanced in post-production. If on-set recording is unusable, actors re-record their lines in a studio — a process called ADR (Automated Dialogue Replacement).

Voice-overs

A voice-over is a piece of narration or commentary recorded separately and placed over the visuals. Voice-overs are common in documentaries, advertisements, trailers, and podcasts. The voice-over artist does not appear on screen — they provide information, set the tone, or guide the audience’s understanding.

Underscore

An underscore is background music that supports the visuals without drawing attention to itself. It sits beneath the dialogue and action, reinforcing the mood of a scene. A tense underscore might use sustained low strings, while a romantic underscore might feature gentle piano. The audience may not consciously notice the underscore, but it shapes how they feel about what they are watching.

Key Fact

The six types of sound creation are: Foley (recreated everyday sounds), ambience (background environment sounds), dialogue (character speech), voice-overs (off-screen narration), underscore (background music for mood), and spot effects (specific one-off sounds synced to events).

Spot Effects

Spot effects are individual sound effects that are timed precisely to a specific on-screen event. A gunshot, a car horn, a doorbell, or a glass smashing are all spot effects. Unlike ambience (which is continuous), a spot effect is a one-off sound triggered at an exact moment. Spot effects can be sourced from effects libraries, created using Foley techniques, or synthesised digitally.

Imagine a scene in a thriller where a detective enters a dark warehouse. The ambience includes distant traffic and a low hum from overhead lights. Foley provides the detective’s echoing footsteps on concrete. A tense underscore builds with sustained cello. The detective speaks into a radio — this is dialogue. A narrator describes the scene — this is a voice-over. A door slams shut behind them — this is a spot effect. All six types work together to create a convincing, immersive experience.

Key Fact

Foley and spot effects are different. Foley recreates everyday, continuous sounds performed in sync with visuals (e.g. footsteps, clothing rustle). Spot effects are single, precisely timed events (e.g. an explosion, a phone ring). Foley is always performed live; spot effects may come from libraries, synthesis, or Foley.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of ambience?
A) A character saying 'hello'
B) Background traffic noise in a city scene
C) A doorbell ringing at a specific moment
D) A piano melody playing under dialogue
practice_questions.marks: B — Background traffic noise in a city scene (1 mark). Ambience is continuous background sound that establishes the environment.

practice_questions.text: Identify two forms of media that rely entirely on sound without any visual element.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each correct form (max 2): radio broadcasts (1), podcasts (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of Foley in a media production. Include an example.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Foley is the recreation of everyday sounds (1). It is performed in a studio by a Foley artist (1). Sounds are created in sync with the visuals (1). Example: walking on gravel to create footstep sounds (1). It enhances realism in the final production (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between underscore and spot effects, using examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with reasoning (max 4): Underscore is continuous background music that supports mood (1), e.g. tense strings during a chase scene (1). Spot effects are individual sounds timed to specific events (1), e.g. a gunshot or door slam (1). Underscore runs throughout a scene while spot effects are one-off moments (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a sound designer might use different types of sound creation to build atmosphere in a horror video game.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis covering multiple sound types with clear links to how they create horror atmosphere. E.g. Dark, low-frequency ambience (wind, distant groaning) establishes unease. Foley footsteps on creaky floorboards make the player feel present. A tense underscore with dissonant strings builds dread. Spot effects like sudden door slams or screams create jump scares. Interactive sound design means these respond to player actions in real time, increasing immersion.
Mid band (3-4): Some analysis with at least two sound types linked to atmosphere, but less detailed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound in games with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: Sound creation is used in many different forms of media. Choose two contrasting forms of media and discuss how the requirements for sound creation differ between them. Refer to specific types of sound creation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion of two clearly contrasting media forms with specific references to sound creation types. E.g. Compares film (uses all six types: Foley, ambience, dialogue, voice-over, underscore, spot effects, all pre-mixed for fixed playback) with video games (requires interactive/adaptive sound that responds to player actions, ambience must loop seamlessly, spot effects must trigger dynamically). Well-structured with clear reasoning.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good comparison with several specific examples but less detailed analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about two media forms but limited comparison or fewer specific types referenced.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound in media with little comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT a stage of the ADSR envelope?
A) Attack
B) Decay
C) Sustain
D) Reverb
practice_questions.marks: D — Reverb (1 mark). The four stages are Attack, Decay, Sustain, and Release.

practice_questions.text: Identify two sources of effects libraries that a sound designer could use.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each (max 2): commercial libraries (1), online libraries (1), DAW loops/built-in libraries (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of creating a sound using digital sample manipulation.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Import a recorded audio sample into a sampler (1). Map the sample across a keyboard at different pitches (1). Set loop points so the sample sustains (1). Create a patch/saved instrument setting (1). Apply filters or effects to shape the sound (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of filters and modifiers in sound synthesis. Give examples of each.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with examples (max 4): Filters shape sound by removing frequencies (1), e.g. a low-pass filter removes high frequencies to make the sound warmer (1). Modifiers add movement and expression (1). LFO creates repeating changes like vibrato or tremolo (1). ADSR envelope controls how a sound changes over time — attack, decay, sustain, release (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of using physical props compared to effects libraries for sound creation in a film production.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of both methods with balanced comparison. E.g. Physical props produce unique, realistic sounds tailored to the exact visual (advantage), but require a Foley studio, skilled artists, and significant time (disadvantage). Effects libraries are fast, cost-effective, and offer a wide range of pre-recorded sounds (advantage), but may lack originality and may not match the exact visual perfectly (disadvantage). Most professional productions use both methods.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid points about each method with less balanced comparison.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about one or both methods with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: A sound designer is creating audio for a science fiction video game that features alien environments and futuristic weapons. Discuss which methods of sound creation would be most appropriate and how they would be used. Refer to at least three methods in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion referencing at least three methods with clear justification for a sci-fi context. E.g. Sound synthesis would be essential for alien environments and futuristic weapons because these sounds do not exist in the real world — waveform selection, filters, and ADSR envelopes can create otherworldly textures. Digital sample manipulation could transform real recordings (e.g. a recorded metal clang) into alien sounds through extreme pitch shifting and looping. Environmental recording could capture industrial ambiences as a base for alien landscapes. Effects libraries provide quick access to generic sci-fi elements. Well-structured with specific technical detail.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with three methods and some technical detail.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about two or more methods but less specific to the sci-fi context.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound creation with little application to the scenario.

flashcard_questions.a: Sound that originates from inside the story world — characters can hear it.
flashcard_questions.q: What is 'diegetic' sound in a film?

flashcard_questions.a: Sound that exists outside the story world — only the audience hears it.
flashcard_questions.q: What is 'non-diegetic' sound in a film?

flashcard_questions.a: Dialogue between two characters, or a radio playing inside the scene.
flashcard_questions.q: Give a typical example of diegetic sound in a film.

flashcard_questions.a: An orchestral underscore, or a narrator's voice-over explaining the scene.
flashcard_questions.q: Give a typical example of non-diegetic sound in a film.

flashcard_questions.a: Recorded parameter changes — volume, pan, filter sweeps — that play back automatically.
flashcard_questions.q: What is 'automation' as a DAW arrangement tool?

flashcard_questions.a: A reference point placed on the timeline to label important moments in the project.
flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'marker' in a DAW timeline?

flashcard_questions.a: It lets the sound designer see visuals directly in the timeline, enabling precise audio-to-picture sync.
flashcard_questions.q: Why is video-file import a useful DAW arrangement tool?

flashcard_questions.a: Stacking multiple sounds on separate tracks to build a rich, complex soundtrack.
flashcard_questions.q: What does 'layering' mean in a DAW arrangement?
Which audio export format is standard lossless quality for professional delivery?

flashcard_questions.a: MP3 — smaller file, some quality loss.
flashcard_questions.q: Which audio format uses lossy compression and suits podcasts or drafts?

flashcard_questions.a: MOV — common in professional editing workflows.
flashcard_questions.q: Which video format is Apple's preferred uncompressed-style wrapper for editing?

flashcard_questions.a: To match pacing changes in the visuals — for example speeding up during a chase scene.
flashcard_questions.q: Why might a DAW need a tempo map with multiple tempo changes?

flashcard_questions.a: Music from a character's headphones may grow into a full orchestral arrangement only the audience hears.
flashcard_questions.q: How can a scene transition from diegetic to non-diegetic sound?

flashcard_questions.a: They help navigate to 'Car crash — 01:23' or 'Dialogue starts — 02:05' without scrolling blindly.
flashcard_questions.q: Why are markers especially useful in a long film soundtrack project?

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of non-diegetic sound?
A) A character speaking to another character
B) A radio playing in the background of a scene
C) Orchestral music played to create tension for the audience
D) Traffic noise outside a character's window
practice_questions.marks: C — Orchestral music played to create tension for the audience (1 mark). Non-diegetic sound is only heard by the audience, not the characters.

practice_questions.text: Identify two uncompressed audio export formats.
Describe how a sound designer would use automation and markers when arranging a soundtrack in a DAW.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Automation records parameter changes over time (1), e.g. fading volume or sweeping a filter (1). Markers are reference points on the timeline labelling key moments (1), e.g. 'car crash at 01:23' (1). Both help synchronise audio precisely to the visuals (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between diegetic and non-diegetic sound, using examples from a film or TV production.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with examples (max 4): Diegetic sound comes from within the story world and characters can hear it (1), e.g. dialogue or a radio playing (1). Non-diegetic sound exists outside the story and only the audience hears it (1), e.g. underscore music or voice-over narration (1). Some sounds can transition between the two (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the DAW arrangement tools of layering and automation could be used together to create a convincing storm scene in a film soundtrack.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis showing both tools working together. E.g. Layering: place wind ambience on track 1, rain Foley on track 2, thunder spot effects on track 3, and tense underscore on track 4. Each layer adds depth and realism. Automation: gradually increase the rain volume as the storm builds, automate a low-pass filter on the wind to make it more intense, fade the underscore in slowly to build tension. Automation allows the soundtrack to evolve dynamically rather than staying static.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid points about both tools but less detailed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about layering or automation with limited application.

practice_questions.text: A client has asked you to create a soundtrack for a short animated film that will be shown online and at a film festival. Discuss the arrangement and export decisions you would need to make, explaining why format selection matters for different delivery platforms.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering arrangement (layering, automation, tempo changes, markers for key scenes, diegetic vs non-diegetic choices) and export (WAV/AIF for festival projection — uncompressed, full quality; MP4/MP3 for online — compressed, smaller files for streaming). Explains why different platforms need different formats. Well-structured.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion covering arrangement and export with some justification.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about arrangement or export but limited connection between platform and format.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about arrangement or export with little reasoning.
